content: The morbidity and financial burden associated with skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs) are substantial. Linezolid and vancomycin are two antibiotics frequently used to treat SSTIs, particularly those caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). This study aimed to compare the efficacy and safety of linezolid and vancomycin in treating SSTIs. To conduct this review, searches were performed across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, and EBSCO CINAHL. The search also included contacting manufacturers for unpublished or ongoing trials and reviewing citations from relevant studies and major review articles. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing linezolid and vancomycin for SSTIs were included. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for bias and extracted data. The primary outcomes evaluated were clinical cure, microbiological cure, and mortality related to SSTIs or treatment. Subgroup analyses were performed based on age and MRSA-related infections. Nine RCTs involving 3,144 participants were included in the analysis. Linezolid demonstrated a significantly higher clinical cure rate in adults compared to vancomycin (relative risk [RR] 1.09, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.03 to 1.16). Similarly, linezolid showed a superior microbiological cure rate in adults (RR 1.08, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.16). For infections caused by MRSA, linezolid was significantly more effective than vancomycin in achieving both clinical (RR 1.09, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.17) and microbiological cure (RR 1.17, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.32). No RCTs reported mortality specifically related to SSTIs or treatment. There was no statistically significant difference in all-cause mortality between the two antibiotics (RR 1.44, 95% CI 0.75 to 2.80). However, linezolid was associated with fewer adverse events such as red man syndrome (RR 0.04, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.29), pruritus (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.75), and rash (RR 0.27, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.58). On the other hand, linezolid was linked to a higher incidence of thrombocytopenia (RR 13.06, 95% CI 1.72 to 99.22) and nausea (RR 2.45, 95% CI 1.52 to 3.94). Patients treated with linezolid appeared to have shorter hospital stays compared to those treated with vancomycin. The daily cost of outpatient therapy was lower with oral linezolid than with intravenous vancomycin. Although inpatient treatment with linezolid was more expensive per day than vancomycin, the median hospital stay was three days shorter for patients receiving linezolid. Consequently, the total hospital charges per patient were lower for linezolid treatment compared to vancomycin. In conclusion, linezolid appears to be more effective than vancomycin for treating SSTIs, including those caused by MRSA. However, the evidence is at high risk of bias, as the included studies were funded by the pharmaceutical company that manufactures linezolid. Further well-designed, independently funded RCTs are necessary to validate these findings.
